en: Has, as you should know, such great renown!
Store an old man’s words in your pack;
Children, listen without making me cry out!
I received it from the transmitters of tradition;
I, your uncle, great Bakai,
Asked those who knew!
Yesterday, in the campaign where giants perished,
In the ordeal my noble lord brought upon them,
There were mighty men and lions,
And there was my champion Almam,
Who could read the Chinese tongue!
When they wreaked slaughter among the Chinese,
The Chinese Shypchaidar and
Giant Tiken—
When the leopard Manas, that bloodthirsty lion,
Seized them and ripped their bellies open,
The fiercest of the Chinese,
Kyrym of the red spear—
That strongman Kyrym
Was knocked from his gray mule,
Struck down by my dear elder brother,
And brave Syrgak of Khan Ulak
Cut off his head.
Deprived of his father,
Kyrym’s son Muradyl
Was left behind at that time,
An orphan while still young.
Living as an orphan, he grew to manhood,
Joined the people of the land,
And, I heard, emerged as a formidable man.
The Kara-Kalmak and the Manchus
Were struck with fear, I heard!
Muradyl learned surpassingly well
The sixty burku and the ilin,
And became learned, I heard!
Against those who had suffered humiliation,
He became an adversary, I heard;
Muradyl could bring down rain
And became a weather-maker, I heard!
Across the face of the sloping land,
At the edge where the enemy descends,
He prepared weapons and took up a spear,
And his face too turned wrathful;
He girded on a sword without a sheath,
And like a cloud about to rain again,
His face turned wrathful.
“If I reach the Burut whose homes burned,
I will wreak slaughter;
I will go and avenge
My father, who died,” he said.
He made his home at Kyzyl-Kyya.
When I asked many questions
Of those who had heard and seen,
They said Muradyl was a hero who bestrode the world!
They said he himself was a weather-maker.
They said his fortunes were complete.
They said he was a warrior who knew
The enemy’s stratagems openly and well!
The pine-covered ridge stretching crosswise there
Is that pass of Kyzyl-Kyya;
The hero named Muradyl
Is the one who dwells in that place.
From the flank of the great mountain
A whirlwind arose, I heard;
From the great Chinese people
An army arose, I heard.
Muradyl surpassed
His father in might, I heard!
He set out to bring turmoil
Upon the Burut, I heard;
If the need should arise,
He set out to seize
Half the khanate of Beijing, I heard.
He set out to bring distress
Upon the Burut, I heard!
A crosswise pass and clear water—
Kyzyl-Kyya is a narrow road—
He took possession of it, I heard.
Muradyl surpassed the Chinese
And became a giant, I heard!
That infidel Muradyl
Has a champion who goes out on watch;
Beside Muradyl
He also has his “Kangön men.”
He has skilled men who scout the ground,
And foremost men with open eyes
Who examine the reconnaissance closely.
Külchoro and Kanchoro,
Understand what I have told you;
Say, “Our lion uncle told us,”
Lion-hearted children, heed my words.
Be watchful in this place;
Do not prop yourselves on your elbows and sleep.
The foe you will grapple with is the Kakanchin;
Do not even doze or take your ease!
Accept what I have said and understand!
The one you will contend with is Bakburchun;
My children, understand this.
Beijing is no easy land,
And the Chinese are no people to play with.
It is a capital city with fortifications,
With a people divided into forty branches.
My precious children, heed my words!
Take care over what I have told you;
Cover every one of the choice coursers
With its abai covering!
When you put on those coverings,
Remove their saddles and leave them bare-backed;
Put hobbles on every one
Of the choice coursers and tether them!
You have never yet attacked an enemy,
You do not yet know an enemy’s worth;
You have never chosen and ridden a courser,
You do not yet know a horse’s worth;
You have never ridden out on a journey,
You were still raw youths who drank no spirits.
Külchoro and Kanchoro,
You were swaggering, heedless souls
Who did not obey what you were told!
Listen to my words like this,
Or I will open your eyes like umach!
Kanchoro and Külchoro
Hummed away without a care;
They did not value those words of Bakai
As much as the hem of their garments.
They carved rump meat and put in mane-fat;
His boys did not worry,
But threw it all together into the cauldron.
They played chatyrash with a clamor,
Playing games and raising dust.
The rogues who had grown up at play
Kept playing without a care;
They did not value your formidable uncle Bakai
As much as his scabbard-strap.
Without tethering the horses or making ready,
They lay down in the tent they had pitched.
Muradyl’s foremost man—
His ears that heard and eyes that saw,
The champion called Zhöözheldet—
Chose and donned a fine gray coat,
Mounted an unhurried pacing horse,
With a battle-axe swaying in his hand
With blue mail and a felt cloak
Flashing across his broad back.
As the sun was sinking low,
At the spur of the distant mountain,
At a great, jutting promontory,
The sight caught his attention.
The devil take your father, Zhöözheldet—
He loomed like a gray-ridged mountain.
He rode up to the pass
From which he kept watch and looked;
Seeking a safe route through the land,
He looked off to that side—
Within Tüp lay Chaar-Tal,
With no cawing crow in flight,
No croaking raven in flight.
He looked off to the other side—
At Kara-Tal by the Jyrgalang,
On a spur of Boz-Señir,
There stood this dark peril.
A gray-mottled tent could be seen;
When Zhöözheldet saw the tent,
His heart grew deeply troubled.
On this side were fourteen horses,
True, dark-coated thoroughbreds,
With sieve-like lungs and copper forelegs,
Their broad rumps a whole armful,
Coursers bred on spacious land,
True stallions to ride into battle,
With blunt tails and solid hooves—
They were beasts to ride in war.
What kind of men are those accursed ones?!
With muscles like a bull’s back,
Fourteen coursers could be seen;
Every one of the fourteen
Was tied high upon a hitching line.
Those were no ordinary tails and manes;
They were not horses of our people of Beijing.
They would not panic at a battle cry;
Their marks as coursers could be seen.
In the darkness of the moon,
They would not misplace a single step.
Stepping on rock high in the mountains,
They were no beasts that would slip,
Surpassing the wild deer that roam the hills.
They would not tire when ridden on reconnaissance,
Nor grow sore when ridden with the baggage train;
Fourteen coursers could be seen.
“I will withdraw without being seen.
It is the sly Burut himself;
The day-chasing bastard
Has arrived here now.
I will slip away and turn back;
I will tell great Lord Muradyl.”
Zhöözheldet hurried in alarm
To the tent with bronze poles;
Before one could say this or that,
In the blink of an eye,
Toward hero Muradyl
He turned his horse’s head,
And openly told him now
What he had seen and learned:
“My lord and khan, Muradyl,
I saw a vast, empty tract;
I saw men as huge as mountains.
They are no idle wanderers;
They bear a manner all their own,
And to my eyes they looked like enemies!
When I counted them from afar—
